description: Solo team from Tampa, FL for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge: The Next Frontier. I plan to turn NASA open data into a simple, interactive web tool that anyone can understand. Interests: space exploration, data visualization and coding. Working solo for now, but happy to connect with other Tampa participants at the local event.
summary:
RIDGE Monitor is a web app that helps astronauts on long missions assess their own health and know what to do next. NASA sums up the hazards of human spaceflight as RIDGE: space Radiation, Isolation and confinement, Distance from Earth, Gravity fields and hostile, closed Environments. On the way to Mars a message to Earth can take up to 20 minutes one way, so crews must spot health changes themselves.

RIDGE Monitor turns a short daily check-in (14 indicators such as heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, mood, vision changes and dosimeter readings) into a mission-control dashboard: a clickable body map, color-coded statuses compared with the astronaut's own baseline, 7-day trends and clear next steps linked to NASA and CSA sources. One click prepares a report for the flight surgeon that shows the communication delay. It also includes a space weather simulation, a gravity transition check for landing, a mission routine with badges, and offline mode.

Live app: https://helios84.github.io/ridge-monitor/
details:
WHAT IT DOES

RIDGE Monitor is a self-assessment tool for astronauts on long-duration missions. It answers the questions in the challenge: which measurements can be done in space, why each check matters, how spaceflight hazards affect it, when a result needs the crew medical officer or a flight surgeon, and what can prevent a critical condition.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Daily check-in: 14 health indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, stress, exercise, hydration, vision change, dizziness, signs of illness, dosimeter reading), each with simple "how to measure" steps.

2. Personal baseline: values are compared with the astronaut's own normal, because the body changes in space.

3. Status at a glance: Usual, Watch, Act or No data, shown with color, icon and word. Missing data never looks "fine".

4. Guidance: every Watch or Act item gives clear next steps, with source tags that open the original NASA or CSA page.

5. Flight surgeon report: one click builds a summary and shows the expected communication delay for the selected environment.

FEATURES

- RIDGE strip: five hazard tiles linked to NASA's framework.

- Clickable body map with 8 regions: function, spaceflight effects, status and sources.

- Today's indicators with 7-day mini charts and a full trend view.

- Environment selector: spacecraft, space station, rover, Moon base, Mars base.

- Space weather simulation: a radiation spike turns into protective steps.

- Gravity transition check for landing on the Moon or Mars.

- Mission routine with prompts, streaks and badges.

- Works offline once loaded (Earth may be 20 minutes away).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Earlier detection of health changes when real-time help from Earth is impractical, and a shared, sourced language between crew and ground teams. The same approach could help people in remote places on Earth.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty: every health fact is paraphrased from NASA/CSA pages and tagged with its source; thresholds that no source gives are labeled as illustrative prototype values. Safety: no diagnoses or drug doses, and the app says it is a prototype, not a medical device. Privacy: synthetic demo data only, no server, no tracking. Accessibility: status is never shown by color alone; keyboard and mobile friendly.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks, no backend), hosted on GitHub Pages. Developed with AI assistance (Claude) for research, code, UI design and the logo; see README, "Use of AI".

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Synthetic data and illustrative thresholds. Next: wearable sensors, camera input for eye and skin checks, and a crew medical officer view.
